lesson.subject: inquiry
lesson.title: Brand It
lesson.subtitle: Shark Tank | Term 4 Week 7, Session 6
lesson.footer: Shark Tank | Grade 5 Inquiry | Week 7 Session 6

plan.curriculum: Victorian Curriculum Economics and Business, Levels 5 and 6: how businesses use marketing to influence consumer choices; Design and Technologies, Levels 5 and 6: finishing and presenting a product
plan.shape: 15 minutes explicit, 40 minutes team time: a short video on slogans, the 4 Ps on Pocket Pal, a quick round, then teams finish the build while the marketer makes the poster
plan.criticalFeature: marketing is four decisions, Product, Price, Place and Promotion; a tagline is short, catchy and names what the product does for you
decisionPoints: the choice check: the strongest tagline
the exit board: a tagline and a Place for a new product
plan.anchor: Find a problem. Upcycle a fix. Pitch it.
plan.catchUp: Missed Session 5? Say: build, test, fix the part that failed. Ask your team which part they fixed, then help finish it.

studentTools: Each team's prototype and Design and Test Log
manipulatives: A3 paper and textas for one poster per team
Junk tubs, joins and the hot glue station: a parent helper, or you in two 5-minute windows
The Pocket Pal model for the I Do
routineIcons: Write it, chin it, show me
Point to A, B or C
boardSetup: Product. Price. Place. Promotion. written as four columns
Team roles reminder: builders finish the prototype, the marketer starts the poster
videos: The Power of Advertising Slogans, HubSpot Marketing (youtube.com/watch?v=QTl6xUFxyOY)

resources.label: Worksheet
resources.description: Your team's marketing plan: the 4 Ps, a tagline and a poster plan.
resources.title: Marketing Plan
resources.subtitle: Product. Price. Place. Promotion.

example.prompt: Pocket Pal sells for $8. Which P?
steps: Ask: what, cost, where, or how people hear?
$8 is what it costs.
Cost is Price.

items.prompt: A team sells bird feeders made from milk bottles. Sort each card into its P.
cards: a table at the Saturday market
the garden centre down the road
an ad in the school newsletter

Place: a table at the Saturday market
the garden centre down the road
Promotion: an ad in the school newsletter

steps: Product: a pocket from old jeans.
Price: $8. Place: a fete stall.
Promotion: posters and the tagline.
example.answer: Pocket | $8 | fete stall | posters and tagline

answers: what it is, what it does, what it is made from
a price in dollars that covers what it costs to make
where people could get it, e.g. a fete stall
how people will hear about it, e.g. a poster

example.prompt: Write a tagline for a cord tidy.
steps: What does it do for you? No more tangles.
Make it short: under six words.
Make it catchy: Untangle your life.

items.prompt: Jack wrote a tagline. Find the problem and fix it.
work: Our product is a box made from cardboard that holds your pencils on your desk.
items.answer: It is a description, not a tagline: too long, not catchy. Fix: e.g. Pencil Pod: never lose a pencil.
Short, catchy, names what the product does for you.

items.prompt: Sketch your poster plan: product name, tagline, picture, price.
items.answer: A poster plan with the name, tagline, a picture of the product and the price.

resources.label: Extension
resources.description: Early finisher option: price your product so the business makes a profit.
resources.title: Extension: Price It Right
resources.subtitle: Price minus cost equals profit.

sections.title: Work out the profit
sections.intro: Profit is the money a business keeps after paying for what it used. Profit = price - cost to make.

example.prompt: Pocket Pal costs $2 to make and sells for $8. What is the profit on one?
steps: Price: $8.
Cost to make: $2.
$8 - $2 = $6 profit.

items.prompt: Work out the profit on one of each.
The hat clip team sells 20 clips. How much profit do they make?

example.prompt: A cord tidy costs 50c to make. Would $40 be a good price at a school fete?
steps: Who is buying? Families at a fete.
Would they pay $40 for a cord tidy? Unlikely.
A fair price covers the cost and people will still pay it.
example.answer: No: too high for the market. Try about $2.

items.prompt: A hat clip costs $1 to make. Which price is best for kids at school?
items.explain: $3. 50c loses money because it costs $1 to make; $30 is more than kids would pay.

slides.notes: Build day two. One line: today teams finish their prototype and give it a brand people remember.

A3 paper and textas for posters. Hot glue station: the parent helper, or you in two 5-minute windows. Prototypes out of storage before the bell. Cue the slogans video. Print the Worksheet one per team, plus a few Extension and Supported copies.

slides.learningIntention: We are learning how businesses use marketing to make people want a product.
successCriteria: I can name the 4 Ps of marketing.
I can write a tagline for a product.
I can plan how our team will market our product.

beats: POINT to the learning intention.
SAY: A great product nobody hears about doesn't sell. Today we fix that.
SAY: Read the I can lines with me. Everyone, together, on three.
SAY: Fifteen minutes with me, then forty minutes to build and brand.
notes.prep: 15 minutes explicit, 40 team time. SC1 the 4 Ps for all; SC2 a tagline is the core; SC3 the team's plan. Anchor: Find a problem. Upcycle a fix. Pitch it.

slides.title: A few words people remember

visual.label: Watch on YouTube: The Power of Slogans

slides.prompt: Turn and tell: what makes a slogan stick?

notes.answer: memorable, says a key benefit, stands out, positive
beats: PLAY the whole video, 1:45.
SAY: Listen for what makes a few words stick in your head.
ASK: What makes a slogan stick?
20 sec. Turn and tell, partner A first.
EXPECT: short, catchy, says how it makes you feel
SCAN for short and catchy.
80%+ -> cold call one pair: name a slogan you know.
Less -> say two slogans the class knows, ask what they share, re-ask.
ASK: Thumbs: can you think of a tagline you know?
5 sec. Cue: thumbs at your chest... show me.
EXPECT: most thumbs up
trap: thinking a slogan has to explain everything.
Fix: count the words in a slogan they know, student sees it's short.
notes.prep: Launch. 1:45. Uses Volkswagen, IMAX, Apple, Coca-Cola and Nike taglines as examples; talk about the tagline, not the product.
notes.sources: HubSpot Marketing, The Power of Advertising Slogans, YouTube.

slides.meaning: A short, catchy phrase that makes people remember a product.
slides.example: Pocket Pal: hang on to your stuff!

notes.answer: a short, catchy phrase that makes people remember a product
beats: POINT to the word. SAY: Tagline. Say it with me. Tag-line.
SAY: Pocket Pal: hang on to your stuff! Five words.
It says what Pocket Pal does for you.
ASK: Is a tagline long or short?
5 sec. Cue: Everyone, together, on three.
EXPECT: short
ASK: Count the words in Pocket Pal's tagline.
5 sec. Cue: fingers at your chest... show me.
EXPECT: five
trap: writing a description instead of a tagline.
Fix: cut it to under six words that say what it does for you.
notes.prep: One key word. Every team's poster and pitch uses its tagline.

rows: A hanging pocket from old jeans
A stall at the school fete
How do people hear about it?

beats: POINT to each row in turn.
SAY: Marketing is four decisions. Each P answers one question.
SAY: Pocket Pal costs me $2 to make. I'll sell it for $8.
People get it at the fete. They hear about it from posters.
ASK: A poster in the library. Which P?
10 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: Promotion
ASK: Everyone, the 4 Ps.
5 sec. Cue: Everyone, together, on three.
EXPECT: Product, Price, Place, Promotion
trap: Fix: Place is where you get it, Promotion is how you hear. Student says both.
notes.stretch: Why might Pocket Pal sell for $8 at the fete but $12 online?
notes.help: Point to the question column and answer one P together.
notes.prep: The model for SC1. Same Pocket Pal numbers in the Extension: cost $2, price $8.

slides.title: Which P?
slides.pivot: ask the four questions: what, cost, where, how will people hear? then re-ask
slides.followUp: cold call one board: which question did it answer?

items.text: A poster on the canteen door
items.answer: Promotion - how people hear about it

items.text: Made from old jeans, holds a hat and a bottle

trap: calling a poster Place because it's in a place.
Fix: ask whether you buy it there or hear about it there, student re-writes.
notes.stretch: For each one, give your own product's answer to that P.
notes.help: Keep the 4 Ps table on the board with its questions.
notes.prep: First decision point: sorting new marketing choices. Brisk. SC1. Six items, about 5 minutes.

slides.title: Which tagline works best?
slides.prompt: A tagline for a cord tidy. Point to A, B or C.

options.text: A cord tidy is a tube you put cords in so they are not messy behind the TV
options.misconception: writes a description, not a tagline

options.text: The best product in the whole world!
options.misconception: boasts but says nothing the product does

notes.answer: C - short, catchy, says what it does for you
beats: SAY: Check each one: short, catchy, says what it does.
ASK: Which tagline works best?
15 sec. Cue: voices off. Point... now.
EXPECT: C
SCAN pointing fingers, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal, cold call one C: what's wrong with B?
Less -> count the words in A, ask what B tells you, re-ask.
REVEAL after fingers are scanned.
SAY: C. Four words, and you know what it does. Tick or fix.
trap: choosing B because it sounds exciting.
Fix: ask what B says the product does, student re-chooses.
notes.prep: Second decision point. Under 80% means teams read their tagline to you before writing the poster.

slides.title: Finish it and brand it
slides.task: Builders: finish and test the prototype. Marketer: write the tagline and start the poster. Everyone: fill in the 4 Ps.
slides.visualLabel: Finish it. Name it. Sell it.
slides.extendedTask: a finished, tested prototype plus a marketing plan with the 4 Ps, a tagline and a poster draft

notes.answer: a working prototype, the 4 Ps filled in, a tagline and a poster draft
beats: SAY: Read the task, complete each part, check your work.
Everyone, together, on three: Finish it. Name it. Sell it.
TIME 40 minutes. At 20, stop everyone.
ASK: Marketers, show your tagline.
10 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: under six words
CIRCULATE. Ask: what's your price, and why that price?
TIME at 5 to go: clean up, store prototypes and posters together.
trap: the whole team on the poster while the prototype sits unfinished.
Fix: point to the roles on the board, team splits the jobs.
notes.stretch: Extension: price it right and work out the profit.
notes.help: Supported Worksheet: clue questions for each P, a tagline frame.
notes.prep: The prototype must work by the end of today; Week 8 is the pitch. Store posters with prototypes.

slides.title: Show what you know
questions: A team sells cushions sewn from old school jumpers. Write a tagline for them.
Name where they could sell them.

notes.answer: e.g. Snug Sack: school's out, feet up!; a stall at the school fete
beats: SAY: A new product. Work on your own.
ASK: Write a tagline, then where they could sell them.
60 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: a short, catchy tagline; a place to buy them
RECORD who writes a description, or a poster as where to sell.
trap: Sell them on a poster at school.
Fix: none now, record the name.
notes.prep: Exit evidence for SC2, with SC1 on Place. One board per student.

slides.reflectionPrompt: Tell your partner your team's tagline, and why it works.
slides.selfAssessment: Fist to five: how ready is your product for Shark Tank Day?

notes.answer: a short tagline that says what the product does
beats: SAY: Let's read our I can lines together. Everyone, together, on three.
ASK: Fist to five: how ready is your product for Shark Tank Day?
5 sec. Cue: fingers at your chest... show me.
EXPECT: mostly three to five
RECORD teams showing fists and ones. Their prototype comes first next week.
ASK: Tell your partner your tagline and why it works.
20 sec. Turn and tell, partner B first.
EXPECT: it's short and says what it does
notes.prep: Next week: the pitch. Teams with an unfinished prototype finish it in the first 10 minutes. SC2.
